original_title: Beyond motivated reasoning: Hostile reactions to critical comments from the outgroup
original_authors: Thürmer, J. Lukas; McCrea, Sean M.
replication_study: single study (registered report experiment)
outcome: Defensive response to criticism of the ingroup: bonus (0-12 cents) awarded to the commenter at a cost to the participant (primary, behavioural ISE), plus self-reported message motive (constructiveness) and message threat
contrast: Criticism of the ingroup (Americans) from an ingroup (US) source vs an outgroup (Singapore) source (Contrast 1)
description: Experiment 3 of Thürmer & McCrea (2018) found that US participants responded more defensively to criticism of Americans from a Singapore (outgroup) commenter than from a US (ingroup) commenter, withholding more of a costly bonus from the outgroup critic (behavioural intergroup sensitivity effect) and rating the outgroup critic's comment as less constructive and more threatening.
citation_sentence: To ensure a stringent test of our hypotheses, we followed the procedures by Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) very closely. We used the same established manipulation for the classic ISE, self-report measures that are used widely in ISE research (Hornsey & Imani, 2004), and the same behavioural measure.
evidence: Results 4.3.1 (p. 6-7): 'In line with our prediction, Contrast 1 was significant, t(1,455) = -4.503, p < .001, r = .117, indicating a behavioural classic ISE.' ... 'Contrast 1 was significant for message motive, t(1,455) = -15.104, p < .001, r = .369, and for message threat, t(1,455) = 7.081, p < .001, r = .183.' Discussion (p. 9): 'Registered analyses revealed strong evidence for the classic ISE across behavioural and self-report measures'. Limitations (p. 10): 'the classic ISE paradigm (i.e., the US and Singapore conditions) was adapted from and results mirror those of existing research (Thürmer & McCrea, 2018, Experiment 3).'
notes: Self-replication (same authors). Merged in pass 2 from pass-1 rows s1:classic_ise_behavioural and s1:classic_ise_selfreport: under the codebook, several measures of the same claim within one study are one entry, and the self-report and behavioural tests are measures of one classic-ISE contrast taken from the same original experiment. A coder who treats the self-report ISE (classic Hornsey-style finding; items 'directly adapted from Hornsey and Imani (2004)', https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167203261295) as a claim separate from T&M's behavioural ISE would split this into two rows; both would be success. Type: same manipulation, same behavioural measure, same population (CloudResearch MTurk US), procedure followed 'very closely'; deliberate changes were added bystander cells, motive measured before threat, and an identification measure added after the DV — close experiment is plausible; tiebreaker (direct vs close -> direct) applied. Exploratory Johnson-Neyman analyses show the behavioural classic ISE only at identification >= 2.45, but the registered contrast is significant and the authors 'establish the ISE as an empirical fact'. Author first names taken from this paper's byline (same authors).

original_title: Reactions to internal and external criticism of outgroups: Social convention in the intergroup sensitivity effect
original_authors: Sutton, R.; Elder, T.; Douglas, K.
replication_study: single study (registered report experiment)
outcome: Self-reported message motive (constructiveness) and message threat ratings of criticism directed at an uninvolved outgroup
contrast: Criticism of an outgroup (South Africans) from a same-group (South African) source vs a different-outgroup (Singapore) source (Contrast 2, pure bystander ISE)
description: Uninvolved bystanders (members of a third group) also show the intergroup sensitivity effect, judging criticism of a group more negatively when it comes from an outsider than from a member of the criticized group.
citation_sentence: In line with this general norm explanation, Sutton et al. (2006) observed the ISE even among uninvolved bystanders who were members of a third group (bystander ISE). ... For the bystander ISE, the involvement of the ingroup can vary: Sutton et al. (2006) compared criticism between two outgroups (in our terminology Outgroup A and Outgroup B), where the ingroup is neither the target nor the source of criticism. We thus term the resulting effect the pure bystander effect.
evidence: Results 4.3.2 (p. 7): 'As predicted, a bystander ISE (Contrast 2) emerged for the self-report measures of message motive, t(1,455) = -20.208, p < .001, r = .469, and message threat, t(1,455) = 13.341, p < .001, r = .331. Consistent with the bystander ISE (e.g., Sutton et al., 2006), participants ascribed less constructive motives to and were more threatened by between-group criticism than within-group criticism.' Discussion: 'we also found unequivocal support for the bystander ISE in self-reports.'
notes: Kept despite neither candidate coding it (luna56 calls the bystander ISE 'a newly added extension rather than a separately replicated original effect'). The source supports an entry: Sutton et al. (2006) published the pure-bystander finding (criticism between two outgroups), this study re-tests exactly that contrast on self-report with new participants, and the authors report it as 'Consistent with the bystander ISE (e.g., Sutton et al., 2006)'. What is new here is the behavioural bystander test, which gets no row. Ambiguity concerns eligibility/type more than result: the test is framed as a theory test of the norm account, not called a replication. Type: different groups (US participants judging South Africa vs Singapore) and Thürmer & McCrea materials rather than Sutton et al.'s, so close extension (conceptual possible). Author first names not given in the paper. NOT coded: behavioural bystander ISE (no prior claim; the authors predicted its absence); Comparison I vs Sutton et al. (2008, book chapter) 'similar magnitude' (exploratory; bystander ISE larger here); exploratory moderation by identification 'in line with' Thürmer et al. (2019); serial mediation 'confirmed past theorizing'; Source and Target contrasts (new exploratory).

original_title: Economics: An emerging small world
original_authors: Goyal, S.; van der Leij, M. J.; Moraga-González, J. L.
replication_study: Wide replication (Section 3.2; Scopus data, 1970s-1990s)
outcome: Co-authorship network satisfies the four small-world criteria (small average degree, sizeable giant component, short distance in giant component, high clustering) by the 1990s
contrast: 1970s vs 1980s vs 1990s co-author networks (emergence over decades)
timepoint: 1990s network (decade by which the original claims the small world emerged)
description: The co-authorship network of economists (EconLit, 1970-1999) became a small world only by the 1990s, satisfying all four small-world criteria: Economics is an emerging small world.
citation_sentence: This paper both narrowly and widely replicates Goyal et al. (2006). The authors analyze the economics profession in the 1970–1999 period and find that by the 1990s, Economics has become a small world.
evidence: Section 3.2, p. 824 and Table 4: "As expected, the networks differ. ... Despite these differences, by the 1990s, the network satisfies all criteria of a small world." Conclusion: "I replicate all main results of Goyal et al. (2006) thrice: ... and using another dataset and a different network definition."
notes: Result label is clear; the eligibility of this entry is the doubt. Footnote 2 concedes that both databases "cover in principle the same publications", so a second coder might treat the Scopus analysis as a robustness reanalysis rather than new data. I count it because Scopus is an independently compiled dataset with different coverage (52% of EconLit volumes), author-profile disambiguation, and papers with 4+ authors included. Typed close experiment because the data source and network definition changed while population/period (economics, 1970-1999) and analysis stayed the same; close extension (ling26's call) is a defensible alternative. The 1970s Scopus giant component is much smaller (5.6% vs ~15%), but the claim concerns the 1990s. Not coded: the narrow replication (Section 3.1) re-runs the original EconLit data (a pure reproduction: Table 1) and a June 2020 re-extract of the same EconLit database for the same years (Table 2, Table 3, Figure 3). Both succeed, but I treat them as reproductions of the same data, not new data; both candidate coders proposed them as entries (see candidate_resolutions).

Also, in this network, I find a strong negative correlation between the number of co-authors and clustering of a researcher (Figure 4a), but it is not as negative as in the EconLit networks." notes: The author counts this among "all main results" replicated with another dataset, hence success. Kept as a separate claim from the small world because the paper names it explicitly as "the second main result" of the original; neither candidate coder split it out (luna56's wide candidate folds it into its description). Same eligibility caveat as wide:small_world.

original_authors: Goyal, S.; van der Leij, M. J.; Moraga-González, J. L.

description: Among individuals with enlarged lateral ventricles, a distinct subgroup (~27%) shows marked cognitive impairment (EVCI), and this subgroup consists predominantly of patients with schizophrenia (8 of 9).
citation_sentence: In our previous study [6], we performed data‐driven classification based on large‐scale neuroimaging datasets to identify a novel subtype of psychiatric disorders characterized by pronounced EV and CI (i.e., EVCI). ... Yasuda et al. [6] performed a large‐scale data‐driven analysis and found that patients with EVCI constitute a distinct subgroup characterized by a high prevalence of schizophrenia.
evidence: Results/Table 1: 'A total of 18.5% (n = 5) were classified as having EVCI'; 'all individuals classified as having EVCI had a diagnosis of schizophrenia'. Conclusions: 'The present study validated the existence of the EVCI subgroup in independent cohorts. EVCI may be more frequently observed among males and is predominantly associated with a diagnosis of schizophrenia.' Abstract: 'This study validated the existence of the EVCI subgroup in independent cohorts, thus supporting our previous findings.'
notes: Original DOI taken from the reference's pub-id in the source XML (ref 6: e70010, doi 10.1002/npr2.70010, PMID 40011069); the rendered references list no DOI. Only the first three original authors are given ('et al.'). Result: authors explicitly say 'validated' and 'provided additional support for our previous findings'; caveats: EVCI n = 5, cognitive data for only 27/146 EV individuals, no inferential test of the subgroup claim itself (prevalence 18.5% vs original 27.3%; 5/5 vs 8/9 schizophrenia). A stricter coder could call it inconclusive on power grounds, but the codebook says follow the explicit statement. Enumeration: I coded the subgroup + schizophrenia-predominance as one claim, since the paper frames the original finding as one ('a distinct subgroup characterized by a high prevalence of schizophrenia'). Possible additional splits a second coder might make: (a) male predominance in EVCI ('Consistent with our previous study, the present study also revealed a higher prevalence of males in the EVCI group' — 3/5 male, but the EV-non-CI group is 77% male, chi-square p = 0.43, so as a between-group comparison it is not supported); (b) the EVCI vs EV-non-CI comparison pattern (lower current IQ, no difference in premorbid IQ or ventricle z-score; 'consistent with the trends observed in our previous study (see Table S1 ... table 5 in the previous paper)') — the CI/current-IQ difference is true by construction, so I treated these as descriptive characterization rather than separate claims. Replication type: same EV definition (z > 3) and CI criterion, but other cohorts/sites and current IQ also measured with WAIS-IV or the simplified WAIS (the original used WAIS-III + JART) — coded close experiment (equivalent alternative measure). Candidates proposed direct and close extension; both are defensible. Direct: same operational definitions, only different sites. Close extension: 'independent cohorts'. But the population is the same kind (Japanese psychiatric patients and HC in the same COCORO consortium, EV individuals drawn from the same 186-person MRI pool reported in the original), so the context did not change; the only deliberate change is to the measure, hence close experiment. The authors never characterize the replication type. What is new is the cognitive data for the 146 non-Osaka EV individuals.

original_authors: Klingbeil, David A.; Van Norman, Ethan R.; Nelson, Peter M.; Birr, C.
replication_study: single study (Grades 6-8, gated Models 1 and 2)
outcome: Screening efficiency: number/percentage of students requiring further assessment (post-test probability .11-.49) after each gate, and number of tests needed to classify all students

timepoint: after the first screening gate (prior-year state test), as the original's stated benefit; later gates also reported
description: Klingbeil et al. (2019) reported that using interval rather than dichotomized likelihood ratios in a gated math screening model reduced the number of students requiring further assessment after the first gate (46-53% vs 60-74%), with nearly all students classified after two tests (a third test needed only in Grade 6; 1.7% undifferentiated in Model 2).
citation_sentence: In the current study, we sought to replicate our initial evaluation of using interval LRs to estimate post-test probabilities to determine math risk (Klingbeil et al., 2019).
evidence: Results, Differences in Efficiency / Table 3; Discussion, Screening Efficiency and Diagnostic Accuracy: "The added precision of using interval LRs to interpret the first screening test was evident in all three grades. As in Klingbeil et al. (2019)..." but "When post-test probabilities were estimated using interval LRs, the number of students requiring a third test (Model 1) or remaining undifferentiated (Model 2) diverged from Klingbeil et al. (2019)."
notes: Mixed result within the efficiency research question (RQ1). The step-1 reduction replicated in all grades: 39.6-46.2% (interval) vs 64.5-72.1% (dichotomized) needed further assessment. But after Step 2, interval LRs left 26-38% of Grade 6-7 students undifferentiated, whereas the original needed a third test only in Grade 6 and left 1.7% undifferentiated in Model 2. The abstract concludes that interval LRs 'may be best reserved for situations where at least three successive tests are available'. Competing readings: (a) code success, because the original's stated benefit was specifically the step-1 reduction and the closing summary reaffirms it ('the primary benefit ... could be to reduce the number of students requiring further assessment after the first screening test'); (b) split into two rows: step-1 reduction = success, and number of tests needed / undifferentiated after Step 2 = failure. I kept one row because both are reported under one efficiency research question. Type is direct by the authors' own label ('direct replication'), although the design deliberately changed one thing: published LRs were applied to a new cohort instead of being derived on and applied to the same sample.

citation_sentence: Klingbeil et al. (2019) conducted an initial evaluation of whether using interval LRs improved upon the diagnostic accuracy and efficiency of a gated screening framework but the LRs were applied to the same sample from which they were derived. The purpose of this direct replication was to evaluate the screening efficiency and accuracy when applying dichotomized and interval LRs, derived from a previous sample, to a different cohort of students.
evidence: Results, Differences in Diagnostic Accuracy / Table 4; Discussion: "Yet, we found similar sensitivity and specificity values when predicting students' end-of-year proficiency status in math, regardless of the LRs used to estimate post-test probability. notes: The original claim is a 'no meaningful difference' claim. The replication again finds negligible differences (sensitivity +.03 for interval LRs in Model 1, Grades 6-7; identical in Grade 8), and the authors explicitly say this 'corroborated' the original, so this is a success under the null-claim rule. Sensitivity and specificity were not estimated for interval-LR Model 2 in Grades 6-7 because many students remained undifferentiated; that is covered by the efficiency entry. This is descriptive diagnostic-accuracy work, so no inferential test of the difference is reported.

Discussion: "it is not surprising that we failed to replicate the pattern of findings for the target outcomes (exit and neglect)."
notes: Primary preregistered outcome. Exit and neglect coded as separate claims because the original and the RRR report each separately (original exit difference −.65, neglect −.42); footnote 1 notes the original actually tested a commitment × constructiveness interaction, so a coder could merge exit+neglect into one 'destructive responses' claim (result would still be failure). Authors call the project a direct replication; procedural changes (computerized Qualtrics forgiveness measures, written funnel debriefing, some labs translated materials) do not alter that. The manipulation check (prime -> subjective commitment) also failed (.02, CI −.07 to .10) but is a manipulation check, not a claim, so no row. The exploratory correlation between subjective commitment and exit/neglect (original r = −.30/−.29) was reproduced in the RRR (Table 5); not coded as an entry because the RRR treats it as exploratory and not a replication target — a second coder might add it as a success row.

original_title: A genome-wide association study of hypertension and blood pressure in African Americans
original_authors: Adeyemo, A; Gerry, N; Chen, G; Herbert, A; Doumatey, A; Huang, H; Zhou, J; Lashley, K; Chen, Y; Christman, M; Rotimi, C

contrast: minor vs major allele / genotype of each SNP (hypertensive cases vs normotensive controls; BP as a quantitative trait)
description: In the first GWAS of African Americans, several SNPs in or near PMS1, SLC24A4, YWHAZ, IPO7 and CACNA1H reached genome-wide significance for systolic blood pressure (with further top-associated SNPs for hypertension status and diastolic BP).
citation_sentence: In the first ever GWAS in African Americans (all subjects were residents of the Washington DC area), Adeyemo et al identified several SNPs reaching genome-wide significance for systolic blood pressure in or near genes: PMS1, SLC24A4, YWHA7, IPO7, and CACANA1H [18]. ... Therefore, we investigated the association of SNPs identified by Adeyemo et al in an independent population of African American subjects from the mid-western United States.
evidence: Discussion, para 1: "In this sample of African Americans, none of the SNPs evaluated were convincingly associated with hypertension as a binary trait or with blood pressure level as a quantitative trait. Thus, we were unable to confirm previously reported associations between PMS1, SLC24A4, YWHA7, IPO7, and CACANA1H with systolic and diastolic blood pressure." Conclusions: "Results of the current study and others do not replicate previously identified hypertension-related SNPs in GWAS." Tables 2-3: all additive-model and regression p-values non-significant.
notes: Enumeration choice: Adeyemo's SNP findings are coded as one entry. Its headline claim is the genome-wide-significant SBP loci (Methods: 'Among these SNPs, only a few had reached genome-wide significance for systolic BP'); the HTN-binary and DBP top SNPs were sub-genome-wide-significant top hits, not separate claimed findings. A second coder could split the entry into three (HTN status, SBP, DBP), as candidate luna56 did; all three would be failure. Nominal hits (rs12748299 with SBP in normotensives, p=0.002, lost after covariate adjustment and with lower rather than higher SBP; rs2146204 recessive p=0.006, SBP p=0.02) were not significant after correction, and the authors frame the study as a non-replication. The methods differ (targeted TaqMan genotyping, case-control design with low-BP controls, no principal-component adjustment) and the authors do not label the replication type. Coded direct per the direct-vs-close tiebreaker; close experiment or close extension is also defensible (different US region; the authors note admixture and allele-frequency differences). Original DOI from the paper's XML reference list (ref 18).

We confirmed a borderline association (insignificant when considered with multiple tests) of rs17177428 and rs7200009 with blood pressure as quantitative trait among hypertensive and normotensive subjects." Results: rs7200009 SBP/DBP p = 0.04 and rs17177428 SBP p = 0.04 in hypertensives (unadjusted), not significant after correction; Tables 2-3 null.

original_authors: Takahashi, Y; Kou, I; Takahashi, A; Johnson, T; Kono, K
replication_study: Case-control study (513 AIS patients vs 440 controls, Chinese Han, Southern China)
outcome: AIS susceptibility (case vs control status) by allele/genotype at rs11190870, rs625039 and rs11598564 near LBX1
contrast: risk allele vs non-risk allele (T for rs11190870, G for rs625039, G for rs11598564), AIS cases vs healthy controls

description: In a Japanese GWAS, common SNPs near LBX1 on chromosome 10q24.31 (rs11190870, rs625039, rs11598564) were associated with susceptibility to adolescent idiopathic scoliosis.
citation_sentence: Recently, a genome-wide association study (GWAS) was performed in a Japanese population, and three SNPs (rs11190870, rs625039 and rs11598564), all of which were located near the gene LBX1 on chromosome 10q24.31, were reported to be associated with AIS susceptibility [1]. ... In order to determine whether rs11190870, rs625039, and rs11598564 are associated with a predisposition to AIS in Chinese Han population of Southern China, we conducted a case-control study involving 513 AIS patients and 440 control subjects.
evidence: Results, Case-control Study (Table 2): 'All the SNPs were all found to be associated with AIS predisposition, the ORs were observed as 1.49 (95% CI 1.23-1.80, P = 5.09E-5), 1.70 (95% CI 1.42-2.04, P = 1.17E-8) and 1.52 (95% CI 1.27-1.83, P = 5.54E-6) for rs625039, rs11190870 and rs11598564, respectively.' The association between common variants near LBX1 and AIS predisposition found in Japanese population was successfully replicated in this Chinese Han population.'
notes: Coded as ONE entry because the original presented a single locus finding (variants near LBX1; title-level claim) with three SNPs in LD (r2 0.59-0.70 here), and this paper's Discussion likewise states one conclusion ('The association between common variants near LBX1 and AIS predisposition ... was successfully replicated'). A second coder could plausibly split into three per-SNP rows (one candidate set did), each of which would also be success (all three significant, same risk alleles). Result label is unambiguous either way. Original DOI not given in the paper's reference list (references give Nat Genet 43:1237-1240), so original_url left blank. Author list in the reference is truncated to five names (et al.). Replication_type: same SNPs and case-control design in a different ethnic population (Chinese Han vs Japanese) with a different genotyping platform (Sequenom MassArray); the authors frame it as confirming the finding 'in other ethnic groups', hence close extension; 'direct' is a plausible alternative. Sex-stratified analysis found association in females but not males, attributed by authors to low power in the small male subset; not treated as a separate claim. Not coded: the case-only severity (maximum Cobb angle) analysis, which found no association; the paper presents it as a new question ('to determine the effects of these variants on the severity'), not as a replication of a severity claim by the original GWAS. Haplotype/age/sex-adjustment analyses are secondary analyses of the same claim. Earlier Chinese replications [34][35] are cited, not replicated.

original_title: The structure of musical preferences: A five-factor model
original_authors: Rentfrow, Peter J.; Goldberg, Lewis R.; Levitin, Daniel J.
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_study: Study 1 (mixed-genre excerpts, Facebook 'My Personality' sample, N = 1,057)
outcome: Factor structure of liking ratings for 15 s audio excerpts (five MUSIC factors), plus the auditory/psychological attribute profiles that define each factor
contrast: not applicable: factor-analytic structure; compared to the original's factors and to its Table 4 attribute correlations (column-vector correlations)
description: Individual differences in liking for audio excerpts of real music from many genres are described by five orthogonal dimensions - Mellow, Unpretentious, Sophisticated, Intense, and Contemporary (MUSIC) - each defined by distinct auditory and psychological attributes.
citation_sentence: Study 1 was designed to replicate the five-factor music-preference model reported in Rentfrow, Goldberg, and Levitin (2011) and to extend that work by investigating a larger set of auditory and psychological attributes.

The attribute-profile convergence (14 shared attributes) is coded as part of the same claim, because it is how the factors are identified as MUSIC, not as a separate entry. original_url is blank: the paper's reference list gives no DOI.

original_title: The structure of musical preferences: A five-factor model
original_authors: Rentfrow, Peter J.; Goldberg, Lewis R.; Levitin, Daniel J.
original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
replication_study: Study 2 (jazz excerpts; Facebook sample N = 913 and University of Texas undergraduate sample N = 408)
outcome: Factor structure of liking ratings for jazz-only excerpts (whether five MUSIC-like factors emerge) and convergence of their attribute profiles with the MUSIC factors
contrast: not applicable: factor-analytic structure; jazz factors compared to the MUSIC factors via attribute column-vector correlations
description: Individual differences in music preferences are described by five MUSIC dimensions (Mellow, Unpretentious, Sophisticated, Intense, Contemporary) defined by particular auditory and psychological attributes rather than by genre.
citation_sentence: Previous research suggests that the MUSIC factors are defined and differentiated by certain musical attributes that account for significant proportions of variance in preferences over and above genre classification (Rentfrow, Goldberg, & Levitin, 2011). ... The strongest test, therefore, of this hypothesis would be if the five MUSIC factors could be replicated solely using musical excerpts from a single genre.
evidence: Study 2 Results/Summary: "The five-factor solution that emerged in the Internet sample was highly consistent with our expectations and clearly resembled the MUSIC model." ... "The present results supported our hypothesis and revealed five jazz-preference factors." But: "at least four of the five jazz-preference factors clearly resemble the MUSIC factors"; Sophisticated psychological convergence = -.40 (Table 4).
notes: Self-replication. The original did not test within-genre structure, so this extends the five-factor claim to a single genre with new jazz stimuli: close extension, with conceptual as a possible alternative. The citation sentence was revised in pass 2 to the Study 2 introduction sentence that names Rentfrow, Goldberg, & Levitin (2011), the same sentence luna56 used. Result: the authors say their hypothesis was supported and five factors emerged. However, the Sophisticated jazz factor 'showed no convergence on the psychological attributes' (r = -.40), so a second coder could call this inconclusive (partial support). The Internet and undergraduate samples are one entry: they are two samples of one study, the undergraduate sample checks the reliability of the same structure (congruence .96, .94, .97, .68, .94), and the attribute analysis pools them.

original_title: Anchor precision influences the amount of adjustment
original_authors: Janiszewski, Chris; Uy, Dan
replication_study: single study (replication of original Study 4a)
outcome: amount of adjustment away from the anchor in hypothetical price estimates (standardized summed difference scores)

description: In Study 4a, people adjust less from a precise anchor (e.g., $9.99) than from a round anchor (e.g., $10) when estimating prices, because precise numbers imply a finer-resolution scale.
